James A. Garfield. On July 2, 1881, President James A. Garfield was shot by Charles J. Guiteau, a delusional office-seeker angered by his rejection for a diplomatic position. Garfield died seventy-nine days later from complications of the wound and infection, making him the second American president to be assassinated.

The shooting occurred in the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington, D.C. Guiteau was a failed lawyer and office-seeker suffering from delusions of importance. He fired two shots. One passed through Garfield's arm, and the other lodged near his spine. Garfield was initially conscious and seemed likely to recover, but he died on September 19 from a combination of the wound and medical complications, likely from infection introduced by repeated probing.

Guiteau had petitioned Garfield for the position of consul to France and, upon rejection, became consumed with resentment. He believed he had been instrumental in Garfield's election and was owed a position by the patronage system. Guiteau's delusions suggest he suffered from mental illness. He claimed he was acting in the best interest of the Republican party. He was arrested immediately and executed by hanging in 1882.

The assassination sparked public outrage at the patronage system, which had enabled unqualified men like Guiteau to roam the halls of power seeking appointments. Congress passed the Pendleton Act in 1883, creating a merit-based civil service and reducing the power of patronage politics. Vice President Chester Arthur, himself a product of the patronage machine, surprisingly supported civil service reform. The event marks the beginning of the transition from nineteenth-century spoils politics to modern bureaucratic governance.

Garfield's assassination was as much a commentary on American political institutions as on Guiteau himself. The shooting illustrated how the patronage system, a fixture of nineteenth-century politics, created a class of supplicants and malcontents with access to power but no legitimate claim on it. Yet paradoxically, his death led to the repair of that system. In American political history, the Garfield assassination stands as a turning point from the spoils era to civil service professionalization.
